script.opening_words: Marcus makes $72,000 a year, has $6,200 saved, and genuinely believes he's doing okay. He's not. He's just not in trouble yet. He has $8,400 in credit card debt, a $580 car payment, and a bank app that calls his savings on track, which is the financial equivalent of a doctor telling you your cholesterol is fine right before the stress test. Marcus isn't irresponsible. He just lives in 2026, where everything costs more than it did 3 years ago.
script.ending_words: number that transforms you from someone who must endure whatever the world decides to do into someone who can choose what happens next. Build it before you need it because the one thing every crisis has in common is that by the time you realize you should have started, the window is already closing. That's not pessimism. That's just math being honest with you before the world has to be.
script.analysis: Full 16847 canonical characters read. A geopolitical-risk personal finance essay: Marcus with $6,200 savings, Doomsday Clock and New START expiry, conflict and military-spending signals, war and currency history (Weimar, WWII occupation, 1948 reform), capital controls (EO 6102, Argentina, Cyprus, Lebanon), why $100,000 (living costs, relocation, hedge, rebuilding capital), post-crisis opportunity (2008), refugees' inability to pay, crisis assets (gold, physical dollars, bitcoin), an allocation framework and Marcus's path. Verified: Doomsday Clock 85 seconds (closest ever) and New START expiry. Wrong or overstated: Eisenmenger misidentified as a German teacher; remaining-capital range ($62-78K, not $64-83K); allocation bands sum to $80-130K; gold "breaking $3,000" stale; Blackstone 80,000 distressed homes overstated; Cyprus haircut was bank-specific. Several historical facts consistent per analyst recall. Fear framing with "WW3" is speculative. The stored ending is complete.
